paras.text: Domain 02 Lecture — Construction Liens, Insurance, and Bonds

Welcome back. This chapter covers the heaviest single category in the Business and Law section: insurance, bonds, and liens. Eleven of your fifty Business and Law questions come from this domain, so this is not a chapter to skim. The good news is that it is almost entirely a numbers game. The exam wants to know whether you have five or six deadlines cold, whether you can tell the four lien waivers apart, whether you know which insurance policy answers which loss, and whether you know who a bond actually protects. Let's build it piece by piece.

Start with the big picture. Michigan's Construction Lien Act is M C L 570 point 1101 and following. It is Act 497 of 1980. It gives contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, and laborers a lien, a legal claim, against the real property they improved when they do not get paid. Two ceilings apply. First, your own lien can never exceed your contract price minus what you have already been paid. Second, the total of everyone's liens against the owner can never exceed what the owner agreed to pay the general contractor, minus payments the owner properly made through sworn statements and lien waivers. That second rule is the no double payment principle. An owner who pays correctly, with the right paperwork, cannot be forced to pay for the same work twice.
Now walk the paperwork in the order it happens on a real job.

First, the Notice of Commencement. On a residential project, the owner prepares it, but only when someone asks. A contractor, sub, supplier, or laborer sends a written request by certified mail, and the owner then has ten days from the postmark to complete and return the form. If the owner blows the ten days, the owner can be stuck paying the expenses the requester incurs digging up the information. If the owner does not live at the site, a copy must be posted conspicuously at the site. Here is the trap the exam loves: the residential notice of commencement is not recorded anywhere. On a commercial project, it is the opposite. The commercial owner records the notice of commencement with the register of deeds before physical work begins. Residential, provided on request and posted. Commercial, recorded. Keep those straight. One more detail: the residential form must have a blank notice of furnishing attached to it, easily detachable, so downstream parties can use it.

Second, the Notice of Furnishing. This is how people the owner has never met, subs and suppliers, announce that they exist and expect to be paid. A subcontractor or supplier must serve it within twenty days after first furnishing labor or material. Twenty days, measured from the first day on the job, not the last. It gets served on the designee named in the notice of commencement and on the general contractor, personally or by certified mail, and certified mail service is complete the moment it is mailed. If no designee is named, you serve the owner. Who does not file one? The general contractor. Anyone in a direct contract with the owner is exempt, because the owner already knows they exist.

Laborers get their own rules. A laborer's notice for unpaid wages is thirty days, and note the trigger: thirty days after the wages were due but not paid, not thirty days after starting work. For unpaid fringe benefits or withholdings, the deadline is the fifth day of the second month after the month they went unpaid.

What if a sub serves the notice late? This is a subtle point the exam can test. A late notice does not kill the lien. Everything furnished after the late notice is fully protected. Everything furnished before the notice is also protected, except to the extent the owner already paid the general contractor for that work relying on a sworn statement or a lien waiver. So late notice costs you only the amounts the owner already properly paid out. Laborers are the exception, a laborer who misses the wage notice deadline loses the lien for those wages entirely.

Third, the sworn statement. This is a notarized list of every sub and supplier you contracted with, plus any unpaid laborers, showing each one's contract price, the amount paid, and the amount still owing. A contractor must give one to the owner whenever payment is due, whenever the contractor asks for payment, or whenever the owner demands it. A subcontractor gives one to the general contractor on the same payment triggers, and to the owner on demand. The sworn statement is the owner's shield. The owner can rely on it, can withhold what is owed to subs, or pay the subs directly. And hear this clearly: giving a false sworn statement with intent to defraud is a crime, on top of civil fraud liability. Also, if you sue to foreclose your lien, your complaint has to show that you provided a sworn statement if one was requested or required.

Fourth, the claim of lien itself. You must record it within ninety days after your last furnishing of labor or material, with the register of deeds for the county where the property sits. Not with a court, with the register of deeds. Ninety days from your own last day of real contract work. Warranty visits, courtesy callbacks, and punch list touch ups do not restart the clock. The deadline is absolute, no extensions, no good cause exceptions. A sub or supplier must attach proof that the notice of furnishing was served. Then, within fifteen days after recording, you must serve a copy of the recorded claim of lien on the designee, or the owner if there is no designee, personally or by certified mail.

Fifth, enforcement. A recorded lien is not money, it is leverage. To turn it into money you file a foreclosure action, and you have exactly one year from the date the claim of lien was recorded. Miss the year and the lien simply expires. The suit goes in circuit court for the county where the property is located, it is an equitable action, and when you file it you record a notice of lis pendens with the register of deeds. And there is a sweetener: the court may award reasonable attorney fees to a prevailing lien claimant. It can also award fees against you if your suit was vexatious.

Now the residential licensing overlay, which Michigan bolted onto this act to protect homeowners. On a residential structure, a contractor has no lien at all unless the work was done under a written contract with the owner, and any amendments or change orders are in writing too. The written contract must contain the statutory statement about licensing, and if a license is required for the work, the contractor's license number. There is no dollar threshold. A handshake deal on a thirty five thousand dollar remodel means no lien, period. And if an unlicensed person records a lien on residential property anyway, the owner can sue to discharge it, and the unlicensed filer is liable for all resulting damages, including actual costs and attorney fees. The case that hammered this home is Stokes versus Millen Roofing: an unlicensed residential contractor cannot enforce the contract, cannot recover the value of the work in quantum meruit, and has no lien. If you sue on work that requires a license, you must plead and prove that you were licensed.

Next topic, lien waivers. Michigan recognizes exactly four statutory types, and the exam will make you discriminate. Two dimensions: full versus partial, and conditional versus unconditional. A full waiver releases all lien rights, a partial waiver releases only a stated amount. An unconditional waiver is effective the moment it is signed. A conditional waiver is effective only upon actual payment of the amount shown. So the safe practice is simple: sign conditional waivers before the check clears, unconditional only after. Three more waiver rules. One, advance waivers are void. Nobody can require you, as part of the contract, to waive lien rights before the work is performed. That clause is against public policy and invalid. Two, accepting a promissory note does not by itself waive your lien. Three, on residential jobs, if a homeowner receives a waiver from someone other than the claimant who signed it, say the general hands over a stack of sub waivers, the homeowner cannot rely on it without verifying it is authentic with the actual claimant, in writing, by phone, or in person. And the statutory forms themselves shout the practical rule: do not sign blank or incomplete forms, and retain a copy.

Here comes one of the most reliable trap answers on this exam: the Homeowner Construction Lien Recovery Fund. It is gone. Abolished. Repealed by Public Act 147 of 2010, effective August twenty third, 2010. Builders used to pay into it and homeowners and subs could recover from it. No more. If an answer choice describes the recovery fund as a current remedy or a current license fee, it is wrong. The only correct present tense statement is: abolished in 2010.
Switch gears to insurance. The exam tests one skill here: given a loss, name the policy. Three policies, three lanes.

Builders risk is first party property insurance. It covers the structure while it is under construction, plus materials on site, in transit, or in storage, against perils like fire, wind, and theft. Half built house burns down, lumber package stolen off the slab, that is builders risk. Either the owner or the contractor can buy it, the contract should say who, and it ends at completion. It does not cover injuries, it does not cover other people's property, and it does not cover your tools. Tools and equipment ride on an inland marine policy, sometimes called an equipment floater.

Commercial general liability, C G L, is third party coverage. Bodily injury and property damage to other people, from your operations or your completed operations. A visitor trips over your ladder, your crew cracks the neighbor's windshield, a connection you soldered fails a year later and floods the finished kitchen, that is C G L. What C G L never pays for is redoing your own defective work. The your work exclusion means general liability is not a warranty on your craftsmanship.

Workers compensation covers your employees, no fault, and it is generally the employee's exclusive remedy against you. Michigan's thresholds are statutory and the exam wants both prongs. Coverage is required if you regularly employ three or more employees at one time, or, and here is the prong people forget, if you employ fewer than three but at least one employee has worked thirty five or more hours per week for thirteen or more weeks during the preceding fifty two weeks. So one steady full time helper triggers mandatory coverage. Public employers are always covered. And remember the statutory principal rule: if a general contractor hires a sub that carries no comp insurance, and that sub's worker gets hurt, the general contractor pays the comp benefits as if it employed that worker directly. That is why you collect certificates of insurance from every sub before they set foot on site, and why you watch the expiration dates. An additional insured endorsement goes one step further, extending the sub's liability policy to protect you.

Last topic, bonds. A surety bond has three parties. The principal, that is the contractor whose performance is being guaranteed. The obligee, the party the bond protects, an owner or a government unit. And the surety, the company standing behind the promise. A bond is not insurance for the contractor. The surety expects zero losses, and if it pays a claim, the contractor must pay the surety back. The bond protects the obligee, never the principal.

Know four bond types. A license or permit bond guarantees you will comply with a law or ordinance, think municipal permit bonds for right of way or sidewalk work. The state residential builder license itself does not require a bond. A bid bond guarantees that if you win, you will sign the contract and post the required bonds. A performance bond guarantees the job gets completed per the plans and specs, and it protects the obligee, on public work, solely the governmental unit. A payment bond guarantees that subs, suppliers, and laborers get paid, and it protects only those claimants.

Michigan public work has hard statutory numbers. On any public contract exceeding fifty thousand dollars, the contractor must furnish both a performance bond and a payment bond before the contract is awarded. Each bond is set by the governmental unit but cannot be less than twenty five percent of the contract amount. Why does the payment bond matter so much? Because you cannot record a construction lien against public property. No lien on the courthouse, no lien on the school. The unpaid sub's remedy on public work is a claim on the payment bond. And that claim has its own clock. A claimant with no direct contract with the principal contractor must serve written notice on the principal contractor within thirty days after first furnishing, and must give written notice of the claim to both the principal contractor and the governmental unit within ninety days after last furnishing, all by certified mail. Suit on the bond is allowed once you have gone unpaid for ninety days after your last furnishing.
Time for the rapid fire recap. Say these out loud with me.

Construction Lien Act, M C L 570 point 1101 and following. Residential notice of commencement, returned within ten days of the request, posted if the owner lives elsewhere, never recorded. Commercial notice of commencement, recorded before work begins. Notice of furnishing for subs and suppliers, twenty days from first furnishing, served on the designee and the general contractor. Laborer wage notice, thirty days from wages due but unpaid. Claim of lien, recorded with the register of deeds within ninety days of last furnishing, absolute deadline, warranty work does not count. Serve the recorded lien within fifteen days. Foreclosure, circuit court, within one year of recording, with a lis pendens, attorney fees possible for the prevailing claimant. Residential lien requires a written contract with the license number, any dollar amount. Four waivers, full and partial, conditional and unconditional. Conditional means effective only on actual payment. Advance waivers void. Recovery fund abolished, 2010. Workers comp, three employees at one time, or one employee at thirty five hours for thirteen weeks. Uninsured sub, the general pays under M C L 418 point 171. Builders risk covers the building, C G L covers other people, comp covers your crew, inland marine covers your tools. Public work over fifty thousand dollars, performance bond and payment bond, each at least twenty five percent. Performance protects the government, payment protects the subs. Payment bond notices, thirty days from first furnishing, ninety days from last. No liens on public property, ever.

That is the whole domain. Eleven questions, and you just heard every number they can ask. Run the deck until the twenty, thirty, ninety, fifteen, and one year roll off your tongue, and this category becomes free points. See you in the next chapter.
